fields.title: The Song of Songs
fields.subtitle: Shir HaShirim, “The Song of Songs”
fields.description: The greatest of songs, as its title says: a love poem between a woman and a man, set in the middle of the Bible. It begins with longing — “May he kiss me with the kisses of his mouth!” — and moves through vineyards and gardens, gazelles and doves, a voice calling “Get up, my darling, my beautiful one, and come away”, two searches through the city at night and a wedding day, to the great saying that love is as strong as death and that mighty waters cannot put it out. Read by Jews as the love of God and Israel, by Christians as the love of Christ and his church, and by all as God’s blessing on faithful human love. Set out line by line as the poetry it is, in the Open Word Bible, a new translation from the Hebrew given freely to the public domain, with an introduction to the book’s shape and meaning and a conclusion on where to read next.

qa.question: What is the Song of Songs?
qa.answer: A book of the Old Testament, eight chapters of love poetry in which a woman and a man speak of their longing for each other and their delight in each other, with a group of friends, “the women of Jerusalem”, listening and answering. Its Hebrew title, Shir HaShirim, is a superlative meaning “the greatest of songs”. It is also called the Song of Solomon, and, from its Latin title, Canticles. It mentions God by name at most once, in the last word of 8:6, and is read in the synagogue at Passover.

qa.question: Who wrote the Song of Songs?
qa.answer: The title calls it the Song “which is Solomon’s” (1:1), and the small Hebrew word before his name can mean by, for, about or belonging to Solomon, as the psalm titles say “of David”. Solomon was remembered for composing 1,005 songs (1 Kings 4:32), and tradition received the Song as his, written in the tenth century BC. He also appears in the poem as a figure (3:7–11; 8:11–12), and some scholars think it was written about him, or dedicated to him, by a later poet. Its date is debated.

qa.question: Why is a love poem in the Bible?
qa.answer: Because the Bible honours the love of a man and a woman as God’s gift. Genesis tells of the first man’s joy at the first woman and of the two becoming one flesh (Genesis 2:23–25), and Proverbs urges a husband to find his joy in the wife of his youth (5:18–19). The Song celebrates desire held within faithfulness — “I am my beloved’s, and my beloved is mine” (6:3) — and warns three times not to stir up love before its time (2:7; 3:5; 8:4). Its climax says that love is “as strong as death” and that “Mighty waters cannot put out love” (8:6–7).

qa.question: Is the Song of Songs an allegory of Christ and the church?
qa.answer: Christians have read it in different ways. Jewish tradition long read it as the love between God and Israel; from Origen in the third century through Bernard of Clairvaux and the Puritans to Hudson Taylor, the church read it as the love of Christ for his church or for the believing soul. Many readers today begin with the plain sense, a celebration of human love. These readings need not compete: the Bible pictures God’s love for his people as a marriage (Isaiah 62:5), and Paul, writing of husband and wife, says, “There is a great mystery here, but I am speaking about Christ and the church” (Ephesians 5:32). Many have found that the Song, read truly as a song of human love, points beyond itself.

qa.question: Who is speaking in the Song of Songs?
qa.answer: The Hebrew gives no names or stage directions, but its verbs and pronouns show whether a man or a woman is speaking and to whom, so the voices can usually be told apart: the woman, whose voice is heard most and who speaks the first and last words; the man, who calls her “my darling” and “my sister, my bride”; and the women of Jerusalem, who ask questions and sometimes reply. Readers differ over whether the poem tells a single story or gathers several love songs, and some have seen two men in it, King Solomon and a shepherd.

qa.question: Which translation of the Bible is this?
qa.answer: The Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Hebrew and dedicated to the public domain, printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. Each line of the poetry is set on its own. The reasoning behind each of its sentences, with the Hebrew beside it, is published at openwordbible.org. The introduction and conclusion were written for this edition.

fields.title: Introduction
fields.body_html:
My beloved is mine, and I am his; he grazes among the lilies.

— Song of Songs 2:16

In the middle of the Bible there is a love song. It has no laws, no history of kings, no prophecy of judgment, and it mentions God, if at all, only once. It is a poem of longing and delight between a woman and a man: their first kisses, their searching for each other through the streets at night, their praise of each other’s beauty, their joy in a garden in spring. It is frank and tender and full of the scent of spices. Many readers are surprised to find it in Scripture at all.

Yet it has been treasured by Jews and Christians alike, and some of the greatest saints have loved it above every other book. Rabbi Akiva, in the second century, is remembered for saying that all the Scriptures are holy, but the Song of Songs is the holy of holies. For the Song tells us something the rest of the Bible assumes but seldom sings: that love between a man and a woman is good, God’s own gift, and strong enough to stand beside death itself.

“The Song of Songs”

The Hebrew title, Shir HaShirim, is a superlative. Hebrew joins a word to its own plural to mean the greatest of its kind, as the holy of holies is the most holy place and the king of kings the greatest king. So the title calls this the finest song of all: “The Song of Songs, the greatest of songs, which is Solomon’s.”

The small Hebrew word in front of Solomon’s name can mean by, for, about or belonging to, as in the psalm titles “of David”. Solomon was remembered for composing a thousand and five songs (1 Kings 4:32), and tradition has received the Song as his. He also appears in the poem as a figure, on his wedding day (3:7–11) and as the owner of a great vineyard (8:11–12), and some readers think the poem was written about him or dedicated to him rather than by him. Its date is debated. The title leaves the question open, and so does this translation.

Who is speaking

The Song gives no names and no stage directions. But Hebrew verbs and pronouns show whether a man or a woman is speaking or being spoken to, and whether one person or many, so the voices can usually be told apart. There are three: the woman, the man, and a group of friends, “the women of Jerusalem”, who listen and ask questions and sometimes answer.

The woman’s voice is heard more than any other. She speaks the first words of the poem and the last. She longs, she seeks, she praises, she warns. It is remarkable, in a book from the ancient world, that a woman’s desire is given so large and honoured a place.

The poem begins without introduction, in the middle of her longing:

May he kiss me with the kisses of his mouth! Your love is better than wine.

— Song of Songs 1:2

One song, or many?

Readers differ over how the Song hangs together. Some find in it a single poem with a story: a courtship, a wedding at its centre (3:6–5:1), a time of loss and searching, and a love that has grown deep and sure by the end. Others find a collection of love songs, gathered and arranged so that they echo each other. Some have even seen three main characters, the woman torn between King Solomon and the shepherd she loves. The poem does not settle the question, and it can be read with delight either way.

What holds it together are its refrains. Three times the same refrain has the woman put her friends under an oath:

Swear to me, women of Jerusalem, by the gazelles or by the does in the fields: do not stir up or awaken love until it is ready.

— Song of Songs 2:7

The same words return at 3:5 and 8:4, and each time they close a section. Love has its own time; it is not to be forced or hurried. Another refrain speaks of belonging: “My beloved is mine, and I am his” (2:16), turned around in 6:3, “I am my beloved’s, and my beloved is mine”, and deepened at last in 7:10. A third pictures the embrace: “His left arm is under my head, and his right arm holds me close” (2:6; 8:3).

Twice the woman searches through the city at night for “the one my soul loves” (3:1–4; 5:2–8). The first time she finds him. The second time she hesitates to open the door, and when she does he has gone; the watchmen beat her, and she can only ask her friends to tell him “I am faint with love.” The Song knows that love includes absence and longing as well as joy.

A garden in spring

The language of the Song comes from the countryside: vineyards and orchards, gazelles and doves, lilies and pomegranates, myrrh and frankincense, the mountains of Lebanon and the vineyards of En-gedi. Its lovers praise each other by comparison, and the comparisons are not always the ones a modern reader would choose. To be told that your hair is like a flock of goats pouring down a mountainside, or your neck like the tower of David, was high praise in ancient Israel, where these were pictures of grace and strength.

In one of its loveliest passages the man calls the woman out into the new season:

For see, the winter is past; the rain is over and gone. Flowers are appearing in the land; the season of singing has come, and the cooing of the turtledove is heard in our land.

— Song of Songs 2:11–12

He calls her “a garden locked up, a spring shut up, a fountain sealed” (4:12), and she answers by inviting him in: “Let my beloved come into his garden and taste its choice fruits” (4:16). Many readers have heard in these gardens an echo of Eden. In Genesis, after the fall, the woman was told, “Your desire will be for your husband, and he will rule over you” (Genesis 3:16). In the Song she says, “I am my beloved’s, and his desire is for me” (7:10). Here, for a moment, love is mutual delight again, as it was in the first garden.

How the Song has been read

Because the Song is in Scripture, and because it speaks so openly of human love, it has been read in more than one way, and Christians still hold different views of how its meanings fit together.

Jewish tradition has long read it as a picture of the love between God and Israel. It is read in the synagogue at Passover, the festival of God’s rescue of his people, and an ancient Aramaic paraphrase retells it as the story of Israel from the exodus onward.

The early church read it as a song of Christ and his church, or of Christ and the soul that loves him. Origen in the third century wrote a long commentary and homilies on it; Gregory of Nyssa preached on it; Bernard of Clairvaux gave eighty-six sermons on it and had reached only the start of the third chapter when he died. That reading ran on through the Puritans to Hudson Taylor, whose meditations on the Song are in this library.

Many readers today begin with what the poem plainly is: a celebration of the love of a man and a woman, which the Bible elsewhere also honours, from the first man’s joy at the first woman (Genesis 2:23–25) to the father’s counsel in Proverbs to “find your joy in the woman you married when you were young” (Proverbs 5:18). On this reading the Song is God’s blessing on desire and faithfulness within the covenant of love.

These readings need not compete. The Bible itself pictures God’s love for his people as a marriage: “your God will be glad over you with a groom’s joy over his bride” (Isaiah 62:5). Jesus calls himself the bridegroom, and Paul, writing of husband and wife becoming one flesh, says, “There is a great mystery here, but I am speaking about Christ and the church” (Ephesians 5:32). Many Christians have found that the more truly the Song is read as a song of human love, the more clearly it points beyond itself.

Love as strong as death

Near the end of the poem the woman speaks the words that the whole Song has been building toward:

Set me as a seal over your heart, like a seal on your arm, for love is as strong as death, its passion as relentless as Sheol. Its flashes are flashes of fire, a mighty flame. Mighty waters cannot put out love, and rivers cannot wash it away. If a man offered all the wealth of his house for love, he would be laughed to scorn.

— Song of Songs 8:6–7

A seal was a carved stone or ring that marked what was one’s own, worn on a cord over the heart or on the arm and never parted with. She asks to be that close, that much his. Then she says what love is: as strong as death, which takes everyone, and as relentless as Sheol, the world of the dead, which never gives back what it takes. No flood can put it out. No fortune can buy it.

The last word of verse 6 ends in -yah, the short form of God’s name. It may mean “a flame of the LORD”, which would make it the one mention of God in the Song: love is a fire that comes from him. Or it may simply mean “a mighty flame”, as Hebrew sometimes uses God’s name to mean “very great”. Either way, the Song ends its great saying on fire.

How to read the Song of Songs

  • Read it as poetry. Read it aloud, slowly, and let the pictures work on you. Not every image needs to be decoded.
  • Listen for the voices. Ask, as you go, who is speaking and to whom.
  • Follow the refrains. They mark the sections and carry the poem’s meaning.
  • Read it with discretion. The Song is frank about desire. Origen reported that the Jewish teachers of his day kept it back from the young until they were mature, and parents may still wish to choose when to share it.
  • Let it lead you to worship. Whatever else it is, the Song is a gift from God about one of his best gifts.

About this translation

The text in this edition is the Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Hebrew and given freely to the public domain. It is printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. The Song is poetry from beginning to end, so this edition prints each line on its own, as the Hebrew sets it out. A few of its choices are worth knowing.

The title. The opening line keeps the name “The Song of Songs” and adds what the superlative means, “the greatest of songs”; “which is Solomon’s” keeps the Hebrew’s openness about whether it is by, for or about him.

Names of the lovers. She calls him “my beloved”; he calls her “my darling”, and later “my sister, my bride”, an ancient term of tender closeness. The women who listen are “the women of Jerusalem”, older Bibles’ “daughters of Jerusalem”.

Love’s fire. In 8:6 love’s “passion” stands where older Bibles have “jealousy”, since in English that word suggests suspicion; and the last word is read as “a mighty flame”.

The Hebrew numbers the verses of chapter 7 one ahead of most English Bibles; the references in this edition follow the English numbering. For the reasoning behind every sentence of the translation, with the Hebrew beside it, see the Open Word Bible itself at openwordbible.org.

fields.title: Song of Songs 1
fields.body_html:
The Song of Songs

The Song of Songs, the greatest of songs, which is Solomon’s.
May he kiss me with the kisses of his mouth!
Your love is better than wine.
The scent of your perfumes is lovely;
your name is perfume poured out;
that is why the young women love you.
Take me with you; let us run!
The king has brought me into his rooms. We will rejoice and delight in you;
we will celebrate your love more than wine.
How right they are to love you!

Dark and lovely

I am dark and lovely,
women of Jerusalem,
like the tents of Kedar,
like Solomon’s curtains.
Do not stare at me because I am so dark,
because the sun has looked down on me.
My mother’s sons were angry with me and made me look after the vineyards;
my own vineyard I have not looked after.
Tell me, you whom my soul loves,
where do you graze your flock?
Where do you let it rest at noon?
Why should I be like a woman wearing a veil
beside the flocks of your companions?
If you do not know,
most beautiful of women,
go out and follow the flock’s tracks,
and graze your young goats beside the shepherds’ tents.

The lovers praise each other

I compare you, my darling,
to a mare among Pharaoh’s chariots.
Your cheeks are lovely between the ornaments,
your neck with its strings of beads.
We will make you ornaments of gold,
set with points of silver.
While the king was on his couch,
my nard gave off its scent.
My beloved is a pouch of myrrh to me,
resting all night between my breasts.
My beloved is a cluster of henna blossoms for me
in the vineyards of En-gedi.

How beautiful you are

How beautiful you are, my darling!
How beautiful you are! Your eyes are doves.
How handsome you are, my beloved, how delightful!
Our couch is green and leafy.
The beams of our house are cedars;
our rafters are cypresses.

fields.title: Song of Songs 2
fields.body_html:
A lily among thorns

I am a crocus of Sharon,
a lily of the valleys.
Like a lily among thorns,
so is my darling among the young women.
As an apple tree stands among the trees of the woods,
so my beloved stands among the young men.
With delight I sat down in his shade,
and his fruit was sweet in my mouth.
He has taken me into the banquet hall,
and the banner he raises over me is love.
Strengthen me with raisin cakes;
revive me with apples,
for I am faint with love.
His left arm is under my head,
and his right arm holds me close.
Swear to me, women of Jerusalem, by the gazelles
or by the does in the fields:
do not stir up or awaken love until it is ready.

Come away, my darling

Listen! My beloved!
Look, here he comes,
leaping over the mountains,
bounding over the hills.
My beloved is like a gazelle
or a young stag.
There he stands behind our wall,
looking in through the windows,
peering through the lattice.
My beloved spoke to me and said,
“Get up, my darling, my beautiful one, and come away.
For see, the winter is past;
the rain is over and gone.
Flowers are appearing in the land;
the season of singing has come,
and the cooing of the turtledove is heard in our land.
The fig tree is ripening its early figs,
and the blossoming vines spread their fragrance.
Get up, my darling, my beautiful one, and come away.”

My dove in the clefts of the rock

My dove, hidden in the clefts of the rock, in the shelter of the cliff,
show me your face,
let me hear you speak,
for your voice is sweet and your face is lovely.

The little foxes

Catch the foxes for us,
the little foxes that spoil vineyards,
for our vineyards are blossoming.
My beloved is mine, and I am his;
he grazes among the lilies.
Until the day breathes
and the shadows flee,
turn, my beloved, be like a gazelle or a young stag on Bether’s mountains.

fields.title: Song of Songs 3
fields.body_html:
A search by night

Night after night on my bed
I looked for the one my soul loves;
I looked for him but did not find him.
I will get up now and go around the city,
through the streets and the squares;
I will search for the one my soul loves.
I searched for him but did not find him.
The watchmen found me as they made their rounds in the city.
“Have you seen the one my soul loves?”
I had hardly passed them
when I found the one my soul loves.
I took hold of him and did not let go of him
until I had brought him home to my mother’s house,
into the bedroom of the one who conceived me.
Swear to me, women of Jerusalem, by the gazelles
or by the does in the fields:
do not stir up or awaken love until it is ready.

A procession from the wilderness

Who is this coming up from the desert
like columns of smoke,
fragrant with myrrh and frankincense,
with every spice the merchants sell?
Look! It is Solomon’s litter,
surrounded by sixty warriors,
the best of Israel’s warriors.
All of them carry swords
and are trained for battle,
each with his sword at his side
against the dangers of the night.
King Solomon made himself a carriage
from the wood of Lebanon.
He made its posts of silver,
its back of gold,
its seat of purple cloth;
its inside was lovingly decorated
by the women of Jerusalem.
Come out, women of Zion, and look at King Solomon,
at the crown his mother placed on his head on his wedding day,
the day his heart was glad.

fields.title: Song of Songs 4
fields.body_html:
He praises her beauty

How beautiful you are, my darling! How beautiful you are!
Your eyes are doves
seen through your veil.
Your hair is like a flock of goats
pouring down the slopes of Mount Gilead.
Your teeth are like a flock of newly shorn ewes
that have come up from the washing;
each one has its twin,
and not one of them is missing.
Your lips are like a scarlet thread,
and your mouth is lovely;
your cheeks behind your veil
are like halves of a pomegranate.
Your neck is like the tower of David,
built in rows of stone;
a thousand shields hang on it,
all of them warriors’ shields.
Your breasts are like two fawns, the twins of a gazelle,
that feed among the lilies.
Until the day breathes
and the shadows flee,
I will go to the mountain of myrrh
and the hill of frankincense.
You are beautiful in every way, my darling;
there is no flaw in you.

Come with me from Lebanon, my bride

With me from Lebanon, my bride,
come with me from Lebanon!
Come down from the top of Amana, from the peaks of Senir and Hermon,
from the dens of lions,
from the mountains of the leopards.
You have taken my heart, my sister, my bride;
you have taken it with a single glance of your eyes,
with a single jewel of your necklace.
How lovely your love is, my sister, my bride!
Your love is so much better than wine,
and the scent of your perfumes than any spice!
Your lips drip with honey, my bride;
honey and milk are under your tongue,
and the scent of your clothes is like the scent of Lebanon.

A garden locked, a fountain sealed

My sister, my bride, is a garden locked up,
a spring shut up, a fountain sealed.
Your branches are an orchard of pomegranates
with the choicest fruits,
henna and nard,
nard and saffron, calamus and cinnamon,
with every tree of frankincense,
myrrh and aloes,
and all the finest spices.
You are a fountain for gardens,
a well of living water,
streams that flow down from Lebanon.
Wake up, north wind; come, south wind!
Blow on my garden and let its fragrance drift out.
Let my beloved come into his garden
and taste its choice fruits.

fields.title: Song of Songs 5
fields.body_html:
I have come into my garden

I have entered my garden, my sister, my bride;
I have gathered my myrrh and my spice;
I have eaten my honeycomb and my honey;
I have drunk my wine and my milk.
Eat, friends;
drink, and drink deeply, you lovers!

A knock at the door

I was asleep, but my heart was awake.
Listen! My beloved knocks: “Open the door for me, my sister, my darling, my dove, my perfect one,
for my head is wet with dew,
my hair with the drops of the night.”
“I have taken off my robe;
how can I put it on again?
I have washed my feet; how can I get them dirty?”
My beloved reached his hand in through the opening,
and my heart was stirred for him.
I got up to open the door to my beloved,
and my hands were dripping with myrrh, my fingers running with myrrh,
onto the handles of the bolt.
I opened to my beloved,
but my beloved had turned away and was gone.
My heart sank when he spoke.
I looked for him but did not find him;
I called him, but he did not answer.
The watchmen found me as they made their rounds in the city; they beat me and bruised me.
They took my shawl away from me,
those watchmen of the walls.
Swear to me, women of Jerusalem:
if you find my beloved,
what will you tell him?
Tell him I am faint with love.
How is your beloved better than any other,
most beautiful of women?
How is your beloved better than any other,
that you make us swear like this?
My beloved is radiant and ruddy,
marked out among ten thousand.
His head is the finest gold;
his hair is wavy,
black as a raven.
His eyes are like doves beside streams of water,
washed in milk,
resting beside a full pool.
His cheeks are like beds of spices,
mounds of sweet herbs;
his lips are lilies
dripping with liquid myrrh.
His arms are rods of gold
set with gems of Tarshish;
his body is polished ivory
covered with lapis lazuli.
His legs are marble pillars
set on bases of pure gold.
He looks like Lebanon,
as splendid as its cedars.
His mouth is sweetness itself,
and everything about him is delightful.
This is my beloved, this is my friend,
women of Jerusalem.

fields.title: Song of Songs 6
fields.body_html:
Where has your beloved gone?

Where has your beloved gone,
most beautiful of women?
Which way has your beloved turned,
so that we can look for him with you?
My beloved has gone down into his garden,
to the spice beds,
to browse in the gardens
and gather lilies.
I am my beloved’s, and my beloved is mine;
he grazes among the lilies.
You are as beautiful as Tirzah, my darling,
as lovely as Jerusalem,
as awe-inspiring as an army with its banners.
Turn your eyes away from me;
they overpower me.
Your hair is like a flock of goats
pouring down the slopes of Gilead.
Your teeth are like a flock of ewes
that have come up from the washing;
each one has its twin,
and not one of them is missing.
Your cheeks behind your veil
are like halves of a pomegranate.
There are sixty queens
and eighty concubines,
and young women beyond counting.
But my dove, my perfect one, is unique,
the one and only to her mother,
the favorite of the one who bore her.
The young women saw her and called her happy;
the queens and the concubines praised her.

Like the dawn

“Who is this who looks out like the dawn,
as beautiful as the moon, as bright as the sun,
as awe-inspiring as an army with its banners?”

The grove of nut trees

I went down to the grove of nut trees
to look at the new growth in the valley,
to see if the vines had budded
and the pomegranates were in bloom.
Before I knew it,
my desire had set me
among the chariots of Ammi-nadib.
Come back, come back, Shulammite;
come back, come back, so that we may look at you!
Why do you want to look at the Shulammite
as at the dance of Mahanaim?

fields.title: Song of Songs 7
fields.body_html:
Come back, Shulammite

How beautiful your feet are in sandals, noble daughter!
The curves of your thighs are like jewels,
the work of a master craftsman.
Your navel is a rounded bowl;
may it never lack spiced wine.
Your belly is a heap of wheat
bordered with lilies.
Your breasts are like two fawns,
the twins of a gazelle.
Your neck is like an ivory tower;
your eyes are the pools of Heshbon beside the gate of Bath-rabbim;
your nose is like Lebanon’s tower
that looks out toward Damascus.
Your head crowns you like Carmel,
and your flowing hair is like purple;
a king is held captive by its locks.
How beautiful and how pleasing you are,
love, with all your delights!
You are as tall as a palm tree,
and your breasts are like its clusters of fruit.
I said: I will climb the palm tree
and take hold of its branches of fruit.
Oh, may your breasts be like clusters of grapes,
and the scent of your breath like apples,
and your mouth like the finest wine,
flowing smoothly to my beloved,
gliding over the lips of those who sleep.
I am my beloved’s,
and his desire is for me.

She invites him to the fields

Come, my beloved, let us go out into the country
and spend the night in the villages.
Let us go early to the vineyards
to see if the vines have budded and their blossoms opened,
and if the pomegranates are in flower.
There I will give my love to you.
The mandrakes give off their scent, and at our doors are all kinds of choice fruits,
new as well as old,
which I have saved for you, my beloved.

fields.title: Song of Songs 8
fields.body_html:
If only you were like a brother

If only you were like a brother to me,
who nursed at my mother’s breasts!
Then if I found you outside, I could kiss you,
and no one would look down on me.
I would lead you and bring you into my mother’s house, and she would teach me;
I would give you spiced wine to drink,
the juice of my pomegranates.
His left arm is under my head,
and his right arm holds me close.
Swear to me, women of Jerusalem:
do not stir up or awaken love until it is ready.

Love as strong as death

Who is this coming up from the desert,
leaning on her beloved?
Under the apple tree I woke you;
there your mother was in labor with you;
there she went into labor and gave you birth.
Set me as a seal over your heart,
like a seal on your arm,
for love is as strong as death,
its passion as relentless as Sheol.
Its flashes are flashes of fire,
a mighty flame.
Mighty waters cannot put out love,
and rivers cannot wash it away.
If a man offered all the wealth of his house for love,
he would be laughed to scorn.

Our little sister

We have a young sister,
and she has no breasts yet.
What will we do for our sister
when the day comes that she is asked for in marriage?
If she is a wall,
we will build towers of silver on her;
if she is a door,
we will board her up with planks of cedar.
I am a wall,
and my breasts are like towers;
so in his eyes I became one who finds peace.

Solomon’s vineyard and my own

Solomon had a vineyard at Baal-hamon;
he leased the vineyard to tenants;
each was to pay a thousand pieces of silver for its fruit.
My own vineyard is mine to give.
You, Solomon, may have the thousand,
and those who tend its fruit two hundred.
You who sit in the gardens,
friends are listening for your voice; let me hear it.
Hurry, my beloved, be like a gazelle
or a young stag upon the mountains of spices.

fields.title: Conclusion
fields.body_html:
Hurry, my beloved, be like a gazelle or a young stag upon the mountains of spices.

— Song of Songs 8:14

The Song does not end with a wedding feast or a happy ever after. It ends with the woman calling her beloved to come quickly, like a gazelle over the mountains. After all its delight and union, the last word is still longing. Love, the Song seems to say, is never finished on this side of eternity; it is always calling the beloved nearer.

The question the book leaves with you

The Song asks what love is, and gives its answer in the great words of chapter 8: as strong as death, a flame that floods cannot put out, a treasure no fortune can buy. Then it leaves a question with every reader. Will you honour love as that kind of thing? Will you refuse to stir it up before its time, and keep faith with it when it comes? Will you see in the love of a man and a woman not something cheap or merely private, but one of God’s best gifts, to be guarded and celebrated?

That question matters in every age. Some cultures have made too much of desire, as if it were everything; others too little, as if it were shameful. The Song does neither. It places desire inside faithfulness, “I am my beloved’s, and my beloved is mine”, and calls it good.

Where the Song points

Christians who read the Song have always found that it points beyond itself. Its love is as strong as death; the New Testament tells of a love that went into death and came out the other side. “No one has a love greater than this: that someone lays down their life for their friends” (John 15:13). Paul is sure that not death and not life “will be able to cut us off from God’s love, which is ours in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Romans 8:39). Here, at last, is a love that many waters cannot put out.

And the Bible’s story ends where the Song ends, with a bride and a longing. Revelation sings that “the Lamb’s wedding has come, and his bride has made herself ready” (Revelation 19:7). Its final pages ring with the same call as the Song’s last verse: “The Spirit and the bride say, ‘Come!’” And the church’s answer is the Bible’s last prayer: “Amen! Come, Lord Jesus!” (Revelation 22:17, 20).

Where to go from here

The Song has drawn out some of the most heartfelt writing in the history of the church, and several of those writers are in this library:

  • On the whole Song. Hudson Taylor’s Union and Communion, six short meditations that walk through the Song from the bride’s first longing (1:2) to the last call (8:14), reading it as the story of the soul’s communion with Christ, broken and restored; and the Ochorus Original The Key Teachings of Hudson Taylor, whose chapters “The Unsatisfied Life”, “Communion Broken and Restored” and “Mine Own Vineyard” (on 1:6) open up that book.
  • On the Song and the love of God. Bernard of Clairvaux’s On Loving God, which hears the bride faint with love (2:5) and the bridegroom’s invitation, “Eat, friends” (5:1); and Hannah Whitall Smith’s chapter “The Song of Songs: The Love of Christ and the Church” in Old Testament Types and Teachings.
  • On praying the Song. Samuel Rutherford’s Letters, whose love for Christ, the beloved “marked out among ten thousand” (5:10), is written in the Song’s own language; and Jeanne Guyon’s A Short and Easy Method of Prayer, which prays the bride’s “Take me with you; let us run!” (1:4).

You can also go the other way, from the text to the classics. Every reference to the Song of Songs in this library can be tapped to read the verse, and the Scripture pages gather what the great writers of the church have said about each passage of this book.

And then read the Song again, slowly and aloud, as it was meant to be read. Its invitation still stands, spoken in a garden in spring:

“Get up, my darling, my beautiful one, and come away.”

— Song of Songs 2:10
